Joulewise Advisory Private Limited has carried out an independent Energy Yield Assessment (EYA) of the proposed Hybrid Power Project (Solar + Wind + BESS) consisting of the following project configuration and site, for supply of Firm and Dispatchable RE power under the NHPC 1,200 MW FDRE Tranche-II tender (200 MW part capacity):
Table 1: Hybrid (Solar + Wind) Project Details
Note:
The entire 200 MW grid connectivity is shared across the Solar, Wind and BESS components, being the Contracted Capacity under the NHPC FDRE Tranche-II RfS.
Only the generation meeting the Contracted Capacity is considered for FDRE compliance; energy beyond the evacuation limit is either stored in the BESS or curtailed.
There is no Non-Participating / merchant plant component in this project configuration; the entire capacity operates under the FDRE PPA.

5.3. BESS Augmentation Philosophy

SoH is reset to 100% at the start of Year 11 (mid-point of the 20-year assessment window), then degrades again through Year 20 following the same 10-year fade curve as Years 1-10. This is a SIMPLIFYING, CALENDAR-BASED assumption (augmentation on a fixed schedule), not a compliance-triggered one.

Why Year 11 specifically: this mirrors a common industry convention where BESS OEM augmentation/replacement guarantees are structured around the mid-life point of a 20-25 year PPA term, to sustain capacity/performance guarantees for the back half of the contract. It is not derived from this project’s specific degradation trajectory or compliance margins.

What was assumed for Table 8/9 above: this is a SIMPLIFYING, CALENDAR-BASED placeholder (full reset to nameplate SoH at Year 11), used only to keep the main Hybrid EYA results (Sections 1-4, 6) self-contained. Section 5.2 below replaces this placeholder with an actual compliance-triggered augmentation schedule.
5.4. Compliance-Triggered Periodic Augmentation Schedule (reference only - see note)

NOTE: The augmentation schedule and event tables below were built for the PRIOR single-BESS configuration (Solar 275 MW / Wind 44.1 MW / BESS 200 MW-400 MWh) and have NOT been recomputed for the current two-site configuration (Wind 31.5 MW / Solar Site1 240 MW+540 MWh BESS / Solar Site2 60 MW+200 MWh BESS). They are retained here for reference only and should not be used for this configuration’s actual augmentation planning - this would need to be rerun against the new capacities if required.

Rather than reacting the instant a shortfall appears (which would require frequent, small, operationally disruptive top-ups), augmentation is planned on a fixed 5-year cadence (Years 6, 11 and 16 - Year 1 is the initial build, not an augmentation). At each checkpoint, the SMALLEST additional BESS energy (in 10 MWh increments, with proportional power added at 0.5 MW/MWh to preserve the original 2-hour duration) is sized such that the WORST year in the upcoming 5-year window - i.e., the year immediately before the next planned campaign, when degradation is most advanced - still meets 90% monthly Peak Availability. Since degradation is monotonic, this guarantees every earlier year in that window is compliant too. The same search logic applies to Solar augmentation, triggered on Annual CUF falling below the 34% floor - this was not triggered in any scenario within the 20-year horizon (CUF stayed above 36% throughout even with zero augmentation).

6.  HYBRID EYA SUMMARY
6.1. Methodology

The study is carried out to understand the revenue potential of the proposed project. A rule-based, day-ahead-aware dispatch simulation is used to model the hybrid plant’s 15-minute generation, BESS charge/discharge behaviour and settlement against the tender’s Firm and Dispatchable RE power supply conditions. Main components of the assessment are as follows:
A. Objective – Maximize Revenue Generating Energy
Revenue generating energy  =  Energy Supplied under PPA − 1.5 × Energy Shortfall under PPA + 0.5 × Energy Surplus
Note:
Since each unit of energy shortfall is penalized at 1.5 times the tariff, the weightage considered for energy shortfall is as per the PPA terms.
In order to prioritize PPA supply over the surplus, the surplus is given a lower weightage.
B. Constraints

Annual basis: (a) Minimum CUF under the PPA – any supply below the minimum CUF will be penalized as per PPA terms; (b) Maximum CUF under the PPA – any supply above the maximum CUF will not be purchased under the PPA.
Monthly basis: Minimum monthly availability during the peak hours – any supply below the minimum monthly availability during peak hours will be penalized as per PPA terms.
Hourly/15-min basis: (a) Supply under PPA cannot be more than the PPA capacity in any time block; (b) Total evacuation, i.e. sum of supply and surplus, cannot be higher than the evacuation capacity.
C. Inputs

First-year 15-minute generation profiles of Solar at P50, P75 and P90 (synthesized from the PVsyst monthly output, scaled to 240 MWac at Site 1 and 60 MWac at Site 2, combined for dispatch purposes). Using a deration factor of 0.4%/year, hourly/15-min generation profiles are calculated for the rest of the project life.

First-year 15-minute generation profiles of Wind at P50, P75 and P90 (interpolated from the source hourly resource data, scaled to 31.5 MW), degraded year-on-year at 0.20%/year over the 25-year PPA term.

Profile of BESS including initial capacity, charging and discharging rates, losses in percentage, depth of discharge, State-of-Health schedule for life of the battery, round trip energy schedule. The two BESS systems (540 MWh nameplate at Site 1, 200 MWh nameplate at Site 2) are combined into a single 740 MWh nameplate pool for dispatch purposes; BESS Usable Capacity (MWh) for each year = Combined Nameplate Capacity (740 MWh) x State-of-Health (%) x Depth-of-Discharge (%); this year-specific usable capacity (not the flat nameplate value) is used as the operative energy limit in the dispatch simulation for that year, together with the corresponding year-specific Round-Trip Efficiency.

Both RE Simultaneous Supply (direct 33 kV injection) and ESS (BESS) Supply are metered at the 33 kV level, before the shared transmission path to the Point of Injection (POI). Accordingly, the two are combined FIRST into a single 33 kV total; a flat Auxiliary Consumption of 1.5% per year, together with Transmission Loss of 2.0% per year, is then deducted from this COMBINED total on the way to the POI - not from RE Simultaneous Supply alone.
D. Assessment
Assessment is carried out at P50, P75 and P90. Energy generated by the solar and wind is distributed among the following components:
Simultaneous Supply – The energy supplied immediately to the buyer under the PPA is called Simultaneous Supply.

Supply to Energy Storage Solution (ESS) – A part of the energy generated is supplied to ESS to meet the demand when the generation is unable to meet the peak period demand. A part of this energy is lost due to internal transmission losses and energy conversion losses of the ESS. The rest is used for charging the ESS. The energy that ultimately charges the battery (i.e., after the losses) is termed as Energy for ESS Charging.

Surplus – The generated energy that is in excess to (i) Simultaneous Supply and Supply to ESS on an hourly basis within contracted capacity, and (ii) upper limit of supply allowed under PPA, is the surplus which is available for sale to other buyers.
Curtailment – The energy that cannot be evacuated due to the evacuation limit or stored in the ESS is called Curtailment.

Losses – Losses are the ESS Transmission Loss and ESS Conversion Loss. ESS Transmission Loss is the loss of energy due to transmission of AC power (i) from the generation busbar to the ESS and (ii) from the ESS to the Point of Injection. ESS Conversion Loss is the loss of energy due to (i) conversion AC to DC and (ii) conversion DC to AC and (iii) losses within the ESS.
The hybrid generation is the sum of the above five components.
Supply
Energy supply under the PPA has two components:
Simultaneous Supply – Explained under Generation and Utilization section above.
ESS Supply – Energy supplied by the ESS to meet the supply obligations under the PPA.
6.2. Supply Conditions and Revenue Components
The revenue generated from the proposed project is from three components:

Supply under the Power Purchase Agreement (PPA). As per PPA, the proposed project should meet the following conditions: (a) Annual CUF of the proposed project should be between -15% and +10% of the declared CUF; (b) Monthly availability of the proposed plant should be 90% during the peak hours; (c) Tariff is common for both peak as well as non-peak hours.
Sale of surplus to other buyers. Surplus can be: (a) Unused generation over and above the PPA capacity on the hourly basis; (b) Unused generation over and above the annual CUF + 10% on annual basis.

Note: with the capacities assessed in this configuration (Wind 31.5 MW + Solar 300 MW combined + BESS 740 MWh combined nameplate), the P50 scenario’s Annual CUF exceeds the 44% ceiling (Declared CUF 40% + 10%) in Year 1 only, before annual degradation brings it back under the ceiling from Year 2 onward. This is the ONLY scenario/year in which the annual CUF-ceiling surplus mechanism is actually triggered in this assessment (P75 and P90 remain under the ceiling throughout); the corresponding surplus energy (approximately 1,852 MWh in Year 1) is shown as a separate line item (Sr 13a) in Table 2/13 and the Annexure, and is NOT counted within Energy Sold under PPA.
Penalty for shortfall on the supply as per the PPA supply conditions. This component has a negative impact on the revenue. Penalty is calculated as 1.5 times the tariff for the shortfall energy.

Peak hours: 2 hours within 05:00-10:00 and 2 hours within 18:00-23:00 daily (4 hours total), as scheduled by the Buying Entity. This assessment adopts an illustrative schedule of 08:00-10:00 and 18:00-20:00 pending the actual notified schedule.

Note: Wind energy generation was initially estimated at the 220 kV grid interconnection level, which inherently includes losses associated with transmission lines and power transformers. The generation was subsequently adjusted to the 33 kV level by excluding the transmission and transformer losses. In contrast, the solar generation was directly estimated at the 33 kV level. The solar energy available at the 33 kV level was then considered as the input for battery charging, and a rule-based dispatch approach was employed to determine the optimal battery charging and estimate the overall hybrid energy generation.

Note on methodology: (i) Solar 15-minute generation shape is synthetic (sunrise/sunset-based, inverter-capped), scaled to reproduce the PVsyst-reported monthly energy exactly; P75/P90 monthly shapes are derived by applying the uniform annual P75/P90-to-P50 ratio, as no monthly P75/P90 split was available from the source PVsyst report. (ii) Wind per-MW basis assumes 1 WTG = 3.15 MW; per-MW yield is scaled to the selected 31.5 MW capacity. (iii) Solar degradation of 0.4%/year and Wind degradation of 0.20%/year are applied year-on-year over the 20-year assessment. (iv) BESS: 740 MWh (540 MWh Site 1 + 200 MWh Site 2) is the combined Nameplate Capacity (not the Usable/SoH-adjusted value) - the Usable DC Capacity applied in the dispatch simulation for each year = Nameplate x SoH (%) x DoD (%), together with the corresponding year-specific Round-Trip Efficiency (84.64% in Year 1, degrading per the SoH schedule); SoH schedule assumes battery augmentation restoring 100% SoH in Year 11. (v) RE Simultaneous Supply and ESS Supply are both metered at the 33 kV level and are combined FIRST into a single total before Transmission Loss (2.0%/year) and Auxiliary Consumption (1.5%/year) are deducted on the way to the Point of Injection - both loss categories apply to the COMBINED 33 kV supply, not to RE Simultaneous Supply alone. (vi) Monthly Peak Availability is assessed on an ENERGY-RATIO basis (Actual Peak-Hour Energy Supplied / Required Peak-Hour Energy per month) consistent with the RfS provision that shortfall is calculated at the end of each month.
